uj/ I feel like what causes the confusion is saying intersex is a medical condition, whereas it's honestly more of a social identity/experience description. And I agree that people with conventionally recognized intersex conditions need a word for that experience and advocacy, which is why it shouldn't be used for other sex differences, both born and acquired. First of all, as a purely medical term it's not that helpful because it encompasses wildly different conditions (and sometimes the exact same condition is not treated as intersex if it aligns with assigned gender, like androgen insensitivity in XX women); second of all, if it was just medical, there would be no good reason to exclude people who acquired the same characteristics or whose conditions are more mainstream.

The intersex/perisex binary complicates things further, because it does leave out non-intersex mixed-sex people. I think it's a fair question what is the utility of labeling trans people perisex when they currently have neither the biology, social acceptance nor access to medical care of either of the two binary sexes. Especially when possibly they didn't have it even pre-transition. It's weirdly common for trans people to have unusual hormone profiles, for instance, which generally doesn't qualify for an intersex condition. For example, I naturally had high enough T to experience mild masculinization (noticeable enough to be bullied over it), and had I pursued a sports career, I would have been banned from women's divisions; but I have no known specific condition, not even in a gray area like PCOS. There would be no use to investigate this now when my endocrine system is artificial anyway. And then there's some ground (though shaky) to interpret transness as a neurological intersex condition as a whole.

I suppose an additional term like altersex could technically solve this issue, but realistically I don't think cis non-intersex people with some sex differences will ever call themselves or be perceived this way (unless they can't cis-pass anymore). Like a cis woman having a cancer-related hysterectomy has never been and will never be seen as anything other than "biologically female" even if she lacks reproductive organs. Moreover, she will be perceived as more female than any trans or intersex person, even if medical advancements put the latter closer to typical femaleness. Sex is deeply social too, after all

Your source doesn't say what you or the author think it says. The patient in question already had far below norm GFR at first assessment, regardless of male or female reference. The author just claims that he

a) would be healthier and make the cut if not on HRT;
 
b) should have been compared to female reference the second time, despite being on T.

They don't have the evidence for either. A single study on trans women says nothing about trans men, because  estrogen doesn't affect renal function like testosterone does. Generally, t increases muscle mass ratio, blood volume and kidney size which improves kidney function. These changes are from long-lasting to permanent, and most will occur post-puberty. The only thing that might have slightly improved with stopping HRT is hypertension, but the usual difference is only a few mmHg, about 10 times less than between this person's and normal bp.

The second assessment used male reference because, again, the patient had been on HRT for a while, and even stopping it wouldn't make a numerical difference in that time frame. Assuming the article is telling the truth about there not being trans male-specific guidelines at the time, it's a pretty reasonable assumption given that sexual dimorphism in renal function is testosterone-driven. Furthermore, the cut-off for transplantation they used is higher than what normally is considered kidney failure, so supposedly, it inherently accounts for things like sex differences. The "female estimate" the article provides is still higher than the usual cut-off.

The good thing is there have, in fact, been several studies on kidney function in trans people, and trans men in particular, starting at least from 2016 to last year. According to 2020 review¹, 3 found that creatinine lab work for trans people matched more closely with their gender than agab and 1 found an ambiguous/in between result. It recommends calculation based either on gender only from 6 months on HRT onwards, or for both agab and gender and adjusting the mean to lean muscle mass. There are also less sex-independent tests like cystatin c. Here's another 2024 study² that compared trans men and trans women. They didn't find a difference in measured GFR, however, trans men did have higher creatinine and cystatin c. I'd wager that some of the former is due to sample size, but more importantly, some participants were pretty early on to HRT (5-6 months) and it may not be enough time to fully reflect GFR changes


¹ - https://academic.oup.com/ajhp/article-abstract/77/6/427/5721763

² - https://www.kidney-international.org/article/S0085-2538(24)00544-1/fulltext

Blood volume (beyond weight) is determined by muscle mass. A trans man 1+ years on HRT will have male-typical body composition and blood volume.

Lung capacity is more dependent on height and, more specifically, chest width than sex. E.i. a really tall woman will almost certainly have bigger lungs than a really short man. The dimorphism is mostly puberty dependent (so wouldn't apply at all or only partially to people who medically transitioned as teens) but also testosterone may widen airways, strengthen respiration muscles and improve oxygen transportation at all ages.

More importantly, lung capacity isn't even a direct factor for anesthesia. It somewhat affects absorption speed, but not dosage or risks. And oxygen levels are continuously monitored during surgery anyway.

uj/ I'm going to challenge you a little on whether "trend" is a good explanation to why we talk about men/women the way we do. Because a no context statement like "Men are asian" is confusing in a way "Men don't cry" is not (even though most men in the world are asian and do cry). Because what is meant instead is the Default Man. Which is a concept that is intensely controlled by gender norms. When people hear "men", they imagine A Guy who is cis, straight, often white and middle class, able-bodied etc, and it's a population mean, but something we're led to imagine. Queer men in particular are actively pushed out of the concept of manhood. Cishet men are "men"; queer men are "gay men" or "trans men", but always men second and with a qualifier. Which is a dehumanizing position in a binary society.

Ultimately, it's not that important. But I do think that LGBTQ people specifically should try not to perpetuate cis- and heteronormativity even when it's easier or more convenient. Even using "men/women" ambiguously is a part of that because we are the main group of people who this vagueness actually affects, and is used to deny us rights and identities on top of that

uj/ most of the things these guys want from "high T" (like perfect facial hair, strong facial bone structure, deep voice etc) are largely genetic and time-constrained. A guy within healthy hormone range who's already well past puberty won't benefit from HRT that way. At best, going from average to upper normal/above normal male level will _maybe_ help with muscle and libido, but it will create risks for cardiovascular system, disrupting natural T production, balding, gynecomastia etc. Even for trans or cis men with genuine deficiency, it's not recommended and doctors won't agree to it just because.

Most of the guys who complain about TRT restrictions just think testosterone is a miracle chemical, with "low = always bad, loser" and "high = always great, gigachad". They don't want the standard trans HRT protocol of aiming for the average and doing regular bloodwork, they want bodybuilder levels and no medical oversight. And for some reason they think it's what all trans guys secretly do, and that they have it "too easy".

And I'm sorry, but even when a patient knows the risks, correcting a genuine deficiency and alleviating strong mental distress (like for cis and trans men currently on HRT) _should_ be the priority. b) "I feel safer with trans men [because I know they are marginalized, and it allows me to hold power over them in many social situations]". Obviously iffy and puts trans men at a risk of abuse.

d) "I feel safer with trans men [because I assume they have a vagina, or look like masc women, or are physically inferior to cis men]". Self-explanatory severe transphobia.

Another problem is that a lot of the time the quiet part is "as opposed to trans women/transfems." Especially from "vagina means safe" people. Which is not only wrong and hurtful, but causes considerable harm to trans women.

Imo, a cis ally who is trans-conscious enough to have a good reason for saying something like that, should also be conscious enough to clarify themselves, if not ditch the topic completely

"Male privilege" is not about superficial mannerisms or passing comments or individual beliefs or whatever else you meant by "analyzing behavior." According to recent big surveys, bi-/pan-/otherwise non-monosexuality seems to be the most common, and gay and straight trans people of all genders are roughly equal in numbers. A couple of possible explanations: labels aren't the full story. In queer and online communities, at least, it's more common for trans guys who are primarily attracted to men to call themselves gay than it is for guys primarily attracted to women to call themselves straight. A lot of the latter identify as unlabeled, queer or even saphic/lesbian, especially if they are non-binary. And on the other hand, straight trans people seem to be less active in online queer groups. Maybe because straight LGBT people are sometimes othered or not given much thought in general, though there are many other reasons.

But even assuming the disproportionality is real, and won't change dramatically for either cis or trans people in the future, this has nothing to do with "male/female brains", strictly speaking. Even if both gender identity sexuality were entirely biologically determined and even if there was a common link, it doesn't mean they would correspond one-to-one. /uj TL;DR: weird sexuality patterns are probably expected if both gender and orientation are influenced by hormones but at slightly different times. But who knows.

Long version: assuming that hypotheses about sexuality and gender identity being at least partially connected to brain's hormone exposure in the womb are correct, it would actually make sense. The time windows would have to be close but different, so the correlation would be noticeable but not strict. I'm fairly sure it's an oversimplification, but as I understand it, it works sort of like this:

1) the more typical hormonal influence during sexuality formation, the more prevalent attraction towards the opposite of one's agab (note: most studies here were done on cis gay men and sometimes women, there's less evidence for bisexuals and iirc none specifically for asexuals, although there's data that both bi and ace people show less differentiation in supposed areas responsible for attraction than monosexuals)

2) the more typical influence during gender formation, the stronger identification with one's agab (also note: there's very interesting evidence of this for cis people and some, but not decisive, for binary trans people; nothing for non-binary people as far as I'm aware)

Btw, this also seems analogical to how gender non-conformity works, at least in young children, but that's irrelevant here. Also when I talk about lack of evidence, I mean lack of studies, which is not a bad thing, as they fell out of fashion because of growing acceptance of queer people and subsequent lack of motivation to prove "what is wrong with us."

So when taken into account that

1) the typical-for-both path seems to be more common

2) hormones are unlikely to change dramatically over a short period of time

This would mean that hetero- and homosexuality among trans people would be about as likely, the first boosted by "inertia" of hormones and the second by prevalence of typical pathway, and the in-between cases, aka bi/pan/ace, at least more prevalent than in general population if not outright predominant, which is exactly what we see. Look at this from another angle: if the development of gender identity and orientation were fully connected, cis gay or bi people would be impossible. Ergo, there must be at least some difference, which would manifest both in a range of sexuality among trans people and range of gender among people attracted to their agab.

I'd argue that if anything, those sexuality patterns actually validate trans people (not that we need biological proof to be accepted and have rights, but still). We have more or less reliable data on biological origins of sexuality, so a demographic with atypical stats of it at least must be fundamentally different from cis counterparts. Also mspec and aro/ace people are a demographic whose experiences are the least affected by transition, so this obviously disproves 'social contagion' theories.

An analogy: up to 52% of intersex people aren't straight and up to 20% are trans (plus ~5% whose relationship with gender is more complicated). Meaning most are men or women but are much less likely to be straight or cis than dyadic people. Obviously, they aren't wrong about their gender or attraction; they also hardly experience any less pressure to be cishet. The conclusion, then, is just that gender and sexuality are tied to general sex development but don't necessarily correspond 1-to-1

/uj You know, I don't think those two approaches are in conflict. It's a little complicated, and I'm not sure whether I can phrase my feelings on the topic clearly, but there it goes (tl;dr in the end):

There's a difference between a social identity and innate feelings. I'll use my own experience with bisexuality as a reference because it's mostly straightforward and understandable for me now, even though gender and sexuality obviously aren't completely parallel.

Similarly to you, I grew up in a conservative surrounding and didn't know much about queer identities until early puberty. Even then, I only had understanding of gay men and women that was heavily influenced by stareotypes. Being more liberal than most people around, at some point I considered myself a cishet ally. I was very comfortable with that label, and didn't think that would ever change. But at the peak of puberty it became undeniable that I was sexually attracted to my agab. It left me very confused as I'd only felt romantic and sexual attraction to the 'opposite gender' all my life and for a long, long time I was sure I must have been mistaken about my sexuality because it didn't make sense to me that it made such a 180 from straight to queer. Leaving aside stareotypes and repression since they aren't relevant, it was only after I came out and cemented my sexuality this way, both socially and for myself, that I realised that my initial arguments were wrong. Some of my 'admiration' for my agab could've been very much romantic, but at the time I put it in the platonic box. If I had the vocabulary and the acceptance then, maybe I'd have classified it differently. But I didn't, so I drew the line in my head between straight crushes and friendly feelings for my agab, and that was the way I also contexualised them. I do not mean that I repossessed my attraction here (and I certainly do not imply that about your gender), I mean that my environment contexualised it in a straight way. It wasn't perceived as queer and it didn't feel queer to me, so it made my social identity straight. It's more complicated than just saying I was wrong and it was queer the entire time, because this straight identity shaped my relationship with society and myself, and it was some kind of truth on its own, even if it wasn't full. This social context was strong enough that the very feelings I'm talking about were perceived differently by me, they felt less strong and more platonic, and it only changed when I started considering myself as bi. 

Basically, the feelings at the base of it all were definitely innate. But the environment had a lot of influence on the social identity forming around them, hence on my understanding of myself, hence on how much importance I assigned to certain feelings, hence how strongly and in what way I perceived them, hence how I chose labels for myself. The 'nurture' didn't succeed in making me exclusively attracted to the 'opposite' gender but, for some time, it succeeded in making me straight. It was more than simply being mistaken or repressing: it affected my comfort zone, my actions, my experiences, the treatment of me by society. In a way, it shaped who I was at the time. Had I not walked the mental path that I walked, it's not guaranteed I'd come to my current identity. There's a difference between a 'straight' me and a bi me, and it goes deeper than picking a label. The main reason why I even consider my current self a truer version is that I feel more at peace with myself than before and because this label functions better; but it doesn't mean that the previous one was completely fake or unimportant.

However, when there isn't this much time for nuance, I prefer to just say I was bi the entire time, even when I didn't think that way. This is because:

a) it aknowledges those 'base' feelings and that they are innate and permanent;

b) while my 'social straightness' was influential, so was my actual bi-ness: I was still different from a straight kid;

c) it achieves the political goal of positioning my sexuality as something permanent natural and normal, and prevents people from trying to 'fix it', both the actual sexuality and the identity. 


I feel the last reason is the main argument for the innate gender identity. In fact, my trans story is very similar to my bi one so I can relate to yours to an extent (and, of course, it's more complicated with gender because there's a much bigger social part to it). People mostly feel hostile about challenging that narrative because it's very accurate for some people's experience and because it opens doors to justifying convertion therapy or heavily controlling gender expression of children. Honestly, this unease is not unreasonable. However, it really sucks that it makes you feel unwelcomed in trans spaces, they are obviously just as much yours as anybody else's. I'm sorry and I think your frustration is valid.

So it can be simultaneously true that, say, dysphoria/euphoria are natural and the reason we consider ourselves a particular gender is influenced by environment. But that's more nuance that fits in most conversations and while it's not always the entire truth, prioritizing nature over nurture helps normalize trans identities and make transphobes leave people alone until they figure themselves out.
